title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: grant non-imputation beatitude; contested origin-vice as proper penalty
pass_a_gloss: The Psalmist testifies in general that one is blessed to whom sin is not imputed—namely what one committed or has in oneself; but he does not teach which sin may or may not rightly be imputed to us. That one to whom sin is imputed is miserable—Placeus grants. If that is true of every sin in general, it is true also of original sin contracted in Adam—granted too. You subjoin that origin's vice is the penalty of the first parents' first sin; and since you mean penalty properly so called, that is the very point in dispute between you.
pass_b_english: The Psalmist testifies in general that one is blessed to whom sin is not imputed—namely, what one either committed or has in oneself; but which sin can rightly be imputed to us, or not imputed, he does not teach. You prove that one to whom sin is imputed is miserable: I concede. You add, if this is true in general of every sin, it is true also of original sin, which we contracted in Adam, and which seems to have had to be said from Adam. I concede this too. You subjoin that that vice of origin is the penalty of the first parents' first sin; and that, since you understand penalty properly so called, is the very thing which is in question between us.
source_text: Testatur Psaltes in genere beatum esse, cui peccatum non imputatur, nempe, quod vel commisit, vel in se habet; quod autem peccatum nobis possit jure imputari, vel non imputari non docet. Probas miserum esse cui peccatum imputatur, Concedo. Addis, si hoc verum est in genere de omni peccato, verum etiam esse de peccato originali, quod in Adamo contraximus, ab Adamo dicendum fuisse videtur. Concedo hoc quoque. Subjicis, vitium illud originis esse poenam primi peccati primorum parentum; id, quoniam poenam proprie dictam intelligis, id ipsum est quod inter nos quaeritur.
